title: Blepharophimosis-Ptosis-Epicanthus Inversus Syndrome (BPES)
summary: BPES is a rare, complex congenital eyelid malformation syndrome characterized by four cardinal features: blepharophimosis, ptosis, epicanthus inversus, and telecanthus. It is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and is frequently associated with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI).

sections.title: Epidemiology & Etiology
content: FOXL2 Function: Transcription factor critical for eyelid development and ovarian granulosa cell maintenance

sections.title: Red Flags: When to refer/screen
content: Amblyopia: Secondary to severe ptosis and visual axis occlusion
Exposure Keratopathy: Due to lagophthalmos post-correction
Ovarian Failure: Mandatory hormone panel (FSH, LH, Estradiol) in adolescent females
Corneal scarring: From untreated high astigmatism/deprivation

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: Stage 1 (Ages 3-5): Medial canthoplasty (Mustardé technique) to treat epicanthus inversus and telecanthus.
Stage 2 (6-12 months later): Frontalis suspension surgery (silicone rod or fascia lata) to address severe blepharoptosis.
Refinement: Lateral canthoplasty if needed for further horizontal expansion.

rows: Hearing loss, heterochromia iridis, telecanthus but no epicanthus inversus

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always measure the palpebral fissure length (normally 28-30mm in adults).
Telecanthus is defined by an increased distance between the medial canthi despite normal interpupillary distance.
Surgical correction should prioritize treating the telecanthus/epicanthus before addressing the ptosis to avoid poor eyelid crease contour.
Genetic counseling is essential for all families.
